client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just... can't bring myself to go, because being around everyone just makes her absence feel even more overwhelming. I'm not sure talking about it is really going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try something.
therapist: Thank you for being here and for taking that brave step to try, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — that quiet courage really matters. The way you're carrying this grief, feeling her absence most sharply in the moments that used to include her, makes so much sense, and it sounds like those family gatherings have become a painful reminder of what's been lost. Together, we can gently explore what those moments bring up for you, not to erase the grief, but to help you find a way to hold it that feels a little less overwhelming.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I appreciate that you're not promising to fix it or make the grief go away, because honestly that would've felt dismissive. But I'm not totally sure what "holding it differently" even means in practice — like, does that just mean I force myself to go to these gatherings and white-knuckle through it? Because that sounds exhausting and I'm not convinced it would actually help.
therapist: That's such an important pushback, and no — "holding it differently" absolutely doesn't mean gritting your teeth and forcing yourself through something painful just to prove you can. Your voice carries a real weariness around that idea, and it makes complete sense, because white-knuckling through pain without any inner shift isn't healing, it's just endurance. What I mean is something more like gently getting curious about the thoughts that make those gatherings feel unbearable — for example, whether part of what's so hard is a belief that being there *without* her means somehow accepting that she's gone.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually... hits closer to home than I expected. Like, if I go and we all sit around the table and life just keeps moving, it feels like we're all agreeing that things are okay now, and they're not okay. And there's something that almost feels disloyal about laughing or having a normal conversation when she's not there.
therapist: The way you said that — soft but quick, like the words were tumbling out before you could stop them — tells me this realization is landing somewhere deep and real for you. What you've just named is so beautifully human: the idea that joy or normalcy feels like a betrayal, like moving on means leaving her behind. But I'd gently invite you to consider — is it possible that laughing at that table could actually be *because* of her, a continuation of what she helped build, rather than evidence that she no longer matters?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's true. But in the moment, when I'm actually sitting there, I don't think my brain is going to make that connection — it's just going to feel like she's missing and everyone's pretending that's fine. I guess I'm skeptical that a reframe like that can actually compete with how loud the grief gets when I'm in the middle of it.
therapist: Your skepticism is completely valid, and honestly it's one of the most important things you could tell me — because you're right that in the middle of a grief wave, a reframe isn't going to magically override that pain, and pretending otherwise would be setting you up to fail. There's something in the quiet, almost tentative way you're expressing this that tells me you *want* it to be possible, even while doubting it, and that wanting matters. In CBT, we don't ask your thoughts to win a shouting match against grief in the hardest moment — instead, we practice building those alternative perspectives gently and repeatedly *outside* of those moments, so they slowly become more accessible when the grief gets loud.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Okay, that makes a bit more sense to me — practicing it when I'm not already drowning in it. But I'm not sure what that actually looks like day to day, like do I just sit and think about my grandmother and try to force positive thoughts about her? That feels kind of artificial, and I'm worried I'd just end up feeling worse rather than building anything useful.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly but quickly, like you're genuinely trying to work this out — tells me you're engaging with this in a really thoughtful way, even if you're feeling a little uncertain and low on energy around it. And no, it's nothing like forcing positive thoughts, which would feel hollow and wouldn't honor the realness of your loss. What it might look like instead is something smaller and more natural — like when a memory of her surfaces, instead of pushing it away or drowning in it, you practice just noticing what it brings up and gently asking yourself what that memory says about who she was to you and what she'd want for you now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That feels a little more manageable than what I was imagining. But I think the hard part is that when a memory of her comes up, my instinct is to just shut it down fast because it hurts so much — so I'm not sure I actually have the capacity to sit with it and ask myself those questions without it just spiraling into sadness. I guess I'm worried that opening that door even a little means I won't be able to close it again.
therapist: The way you just said that — fast, loud, with a kind of urgency — tells me this fear isn't abstract for you, it feels very immediate and real, like you're already bracing against something. That instinct to shut the door quickly makes complete sense as a protection strategy, and it's actually been working to keep you functioning — the worry isn't that you're doing something wrong, it's that the door has started to feel all-or-nothing, like it's either sealed shut or floods everything. Part of what we'd work on together is helping you discover that there's a middle setting — that you can open it just a crack, for just a moment, and still be the one in control of it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: The idea of a middle setting actually resonates with me, because you're right that it does feel all-or-nothing — like I'm either completely avoiding it or I'm going to fall apart entirely. But I guess my worry is, how do I know in the moment when I've opened it "just a crack" versus when I'm already starting to spiral? I don't fully trust my own judgment on that right now, especially when the grief catches me off guard.
therapist: The softness in your voice as you said that, paired with something that sounds like genuine uncertainty rather than panic, tells me you're asking this question from a place of real self-awareness rather than crisis — which is actually a sign that your judgment is more intact than you're giving yourself credit for. That said, it's completely reasonable not to trust yourself on this yet, and the good news is that we don't leave it to in-the-moment judgment alone — we'd work together to build some concrete, simple anchors beforehand, like a specific thought or even a physical grounding action, that become your signal to gently close the door back up. Learning to recognize the difference between sitting with grief and spiraling into it is itself a skill we'd practice gradually, so you're not figuring it out alone in the hardest moments.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think what's helping me feel a little less resistant right now is knowing that there's supposed to be something concrete to hold onto, not just a vague instruction to "sit with it." But I'm also aware that I tend to learn things in theory and then completely forget them when I'm actually emotional, so I'm a bit skeptical about whether an anchor is going to feel accessible when I'm already caught off guard by a memory. Can you give me an example of what one of those anchors might actually look like, so I can start to picture whether it's something I could realistically use?
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, with a kind of bright urgency — tells me you're genuinely leaning in right now, even while holding onto that healthy skepticism, and that combination is really valuable. A concrete example of an anchor might be something like pressing your feet firmly into the floor and silently naming three things you can physically feel in that moment — it sounds simple, almost too simple, but the point is that it's so automatic it doesn't require emotional bandwidth to remember. The reason these physical anchors tend to survive emotional flooding better than thoughts do is precisely because your body is always available even when your mind is overwhelmed — and we'd practice it enough in calm moments that it starts to become a reflex rather than something you have to remember.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That's actually less abstract than I was expecting, and I can see why something physical might stick better than trying to remember a thought when I'm already upset. I think I could maybe try that — but I'm also a little self-conscious about it, like if a memory of my grandmother hits me at a family gathering, am I just going to be sitting there pressing my feet into the floor while everyone else is talking? I guess I'm worried it might look strange or draw attention to the fact that I'm struggling, when part of me really doesn't want anyone to know how much I'm falling apart.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice as you said that tells me this self-consciousness is something you feel quite acutely — like on top of the grief itself, there's a whole layer of wanting to appear okay for everyone else, which is its own kind of exhausting weight to carry. The good news is that pressing your feet into the floor is completely invisible — no one at that table would have any idea it was happening, and that's actually part of why physical anchors work so well in social situations. But I'd also gently notice with you that there's something worth exploring in that strong need to hide the struggle — because the people around that table are likely grieving her too, and sometimes the most unexpectedly healing moments come from letting someone else see that you're not okay.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I know logically that they're grieving too, but there's something about being the one who visibly falls apart that feels really uncomfortable — like I'd be burdening everyone else with my emotions when they're already dealing with their own. And honestly, part of me is also scared that if I let someone see how much I'm struggling, they might say something well-meaning but wrong, and that would almost feel worse than just holding it together. I think I've gotten so used to managing this alone that letting anyone in, even family, feels like a risk I'm not sure I'm ready to take.
therapist: The way you're speaking — very quickly, at a high pitch, even while the words themselves are measured and controlled — tells me this is touching something that feels quite vulnerable and close to the surface, like you're holding a lot together even as you're describing it. What you've just named is so understandable: the fear of being a burden, the fear of a clumsy response making it worse, the safety of managing it alone — these are all really coherent reasons to keep the door closed, and I want to honor that they've been protecting you. But I'd gently invite you to notice that the belief "showing my grief burdens others" is itself a thought worth examining — because it's also possible that the people who loved her are quietly waiting for someone to be the first to say *I'm not okay either.*
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
